issues.item: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you
issues.explanation: For a natural disaster trauma, this appraisal is a poor thematic fit because it implies an interpersonal perpetrator threat ('who will harm you') rather than danger from impersonal environmental forces. The rest of the profile is built around disaster-related ongoing danger/hypervigilance and intrusive reliving, so this item stands out as clinically incongruent with the specified trauma type.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am
issues.explanation: For a natural disaster trauma, the appraisal 'I acted in ways that go against who I am' is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile. The memory and threat items describe classic fear-based re-experiencing and hypervigilance, but there is no accompanying content suggesting perpetration, moral injury, or a specific action during the disaster that would plausibly drive a strong violated-values appraisal.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Failed Role: I have failed in my most important role in life
issues.explanation: 'I have failed in my most important role in life' could occur after a disaster, but here it sits awkwardly with the otherwise generic fear/reliving profile. There are no memory or threat items about failing to protect family, losing dependents, or role-related guilt, so this item lacks support from the rest of the formulation.

issues.item: Threat: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
issues.explanation: 'I need to stay alert' while trying to sleep is more characteristic of an ongoing human threat context than of a completed natural disaster, especially when paired with scanning exits and staying near exits in all buildings. Taken together, these threat items imply anticipation of intentional attack or entrapment rather than the specific threat structure suggested by the trauma type.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Failed Role: I have failed in my most important role in life
issues.explanation: 'Failed Role' is not impossible, but it is the least coherent appraisal in this profile for a 65-year-old married male retail worker with natural-disaster trauma. The rest of the profile centers on ongoing danger, hypervigilance, and intrusive reliving; this item instead implies a specific role-based self-evaluation that is not supported by the other selected appraisals, memory, threat, or coping items.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Other-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what other people have done to me
issues.explanation: 'Other-Blame Rumination' sits awkwardly with a natural-disaster trauma profile. Blame can occur, but this item specifically focuses on dwelling on what other people have done to me, whereas the rest of the profile describes threat and reliving linked to impersonal environmental danger rather than interpersonal harm or betrayal. Without any corroborating appraisal or memory content involving preventable human actions, this item is clinically hard to reconcile.

vignette:
Kofi Mensah is a 65-year-old Ghanaian-born man who has lived in the United States for nearly three decades, working for the past eleven years as a floor associate at a large home-improvement retail store in suburban Georgia. He came to the intake appointment accompanied by his wife, Abena, who sat quietly in the waiting room while Kofi spoke with measured, careful words about what had happened to him - and about what had not stopped happening since.

In the late summer of two years ago, Kofi was visiting family in coastal Louisiana when Hurricane Ida made landfall. He had stayed behind with his brother-in-law to protect the property, both men certain the storm would weaken before it arrived. It did not. The hours that followed were unlike anything Kofi had encountered in sixty-three years of living: the walls of his brother-in-law's house groaning and then partially giving way, floodwater rising past his knees and then his waist in near-total darkness, the roar of wind so absolute it swallowed every other sound. For several hours he clung to an interior door frame, unable to see more than inches in front of him, uncertain whether the structure above him would hold or collapse entirely. When the water finally receded enough for him to move, he found his brother-in-law injured but alive on the second floor. Both men were rescued the following morning. Kofi flew home to Georgia four days later with dry clothes and, as he described it to his therapist, "something broken inside that I cannot find to fix."

In the weeks after his return, Kofi noticed that the memories of those hours would not stay in the past where he placed them. They arrived without warning - not as recollections but as re-immersions, a film that did not merely play but pulled him back into the dark water, the groaning walls, the sensation of not knowing whether the next moment would be his last. During these episodes he was certain, in a way that no amount of reassurance could reach, that it was happening right now. Abena would find him rigid at the kitchen table, his hands gripping the edge, and he would be unable to explain to her that he was not in Georgia at all.

He had come to believe, with a quiet but unshakeable conviction, that the world had revealed its true nature to him that night - that it was irreducibly dangerous, that safety was an arrangement that could dissolve in hours, and that the man he had been before the storm was gone. He did not say this dramatically; he said it the way a person states a fact they have verified repeatedly. He was also certain that he had to remain alert at all times, that dropping his guard even briefly was an invitation to catastrophe.

This certainty reorganised his daily life in ways that accumulated over months. At the retail store where he works, Kofi now positions himself instinctively near the emergency exit at the far end of the lumber aisle - his assigned section - and he has quietly rearranged his work patterns so that he is rarely more than a few steps from that door. When customers approach him, he finds himself scanning the high ceiling, the wide concrete floor, the loading bay doors, cataloguing what might give way and what might hold. He falls asleep with difficulty most nights, feeling that unconsciousness itself is a form of exposure, a dropping of the watch he believes he must keep. He has begun declining invitations to family gatherings held in unfamiliar buildings, and Abena has noticed that he will not sit with his back to a room. A younger colleague at the store mentioned to a supervisor that Kofi seemed distracted and difficult to reach; Kofi received a quiet word about customer engagement that he found humiliating and that deepened his sense that the damage in him was permanent and visible to others.

What finally brought him to seek help was Abena's direct and tearful request one evening, after she found him standing at their bedroom window at two in the morning, scanning the yard. He came, he said, for her. What he feared most was that therapy would confirm what he already suspected - that there was no going back. What he hoped for, almost against his own belief, was to be wrong about that.
